caf.title: CarMax Auto Finance income & penetration
caf.content:
CAF income is the profit from CarMax's captive finance arm (interest income on the receivables it originates and retains, less funding costs and provision for loan losses). Net penetration is the share of CarMax's own retail unit sales that CAF originates (after third-party lenders also offered to the customer).

For CarMax, Inc.: CAF has consistently contributed more than half of consolidated operating profit, so a dip in CAF income (from tighter credit, higher loss provisions, or lower penetration) moves total earnings more than a comparable swing in vehicle gross profit.

What to watch:

  • CAF income falling faster than units sold (rising loss provisions or funding cost)
  • Penetration drifting down as competing lenders undercut CAF's rates
  • CAF income is a slice of segment profit, not incremental cash -- the DCF's owner FCF already includes it through consolidated net income

compGrowth.title: Comparable store growth: units vs revenue
compGrowth.content:
Comp unit growth is the year-over-year change in used vehicles retailed at stores open at least a year -- the volume metric management leads with on every call. Comp sales growth is the revenue-based version, which mixes in average selling price.

For CarMax, Inc.: the two can diverge sharply -- revenue comps can rise on price alone while units fall, which is a weaker signal for store-level volume and operating leverage than it looks.

What to watch:

  • Unit growth turning negative while revenue growth stays positive (price masking a volume decline)
  • Unit growth as the better read on store productivity and market share

gpPerUnit.title: Gross profit per unit: used vs wholesale
gpPerUnit.content:
Used GP/unit is gross profit on each retail used vehicle sold; wholesale GP/unit is gross profit on vehicles CarMax buys at appraisal and resells at its own wholesale auctions. Both are per-vehicle dollar amounts, not margins.

For CarMax, Inc.: CarMax targets a stable per-unit used margin rather than chasing volume at a lower margin, so this is management's own scorecard; wholesale GP/unit tracks appraisal volume and the health of the auction market CarMax does not fully control.

What to watch:

  • Used GP/unit drifting below its historical ~$2,200-2,300 band
  • Wholesale GP/unit compressing alongside falling wholesale prices (a used-vehicle pricing downturn)

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For CarMax, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For CarMax, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For CarMax, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For CarMax, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For CarMax, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For CarMax, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For CarMax, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For CarMax, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For CarMax, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
